sites.name: Black Cloud Mine / Leadville Unit / Irene Shaft
sites.componentType: Major Underground Lead-Zinc-Silver Mine / Shaft & Flotation-Mill System
sites.componentDetail: Black Cloud / Leadville Unit underground mine complex including Irene and Black Cloud shafts, mill and tailings system
overview: The Black Cloud, also known as the Leadville Unit, was a major modern-era underground lead-zinc-silver operation in the Leadville mining district. Its surface and underground system included the Irene and Black Cloud shafts, mill and tailings infrastructure, and connections with older workings in the district.

Remnant treats the Black Cloud as a mine complex rather than a single structure because its history spans underground workings, shaft facilities, ore processing, tailings, and later environmental management.

timeline.text: A joint venture of ASARCO and Resurrection Mining Company reopened the Irene workings and confirmed additional ore reserves in the eastern Leadville district.
The Black Cloud shaft was sunk in Iowa Gulch to reach the newly identified ore reserves.
The Black Cloud mine and mill entered production in April.
Mining History Association documentation identifies the Black Cloud as having been operated by ASARCO until 1999.

moreHistory: Federal and mining-record sources identify Black Cloud Mine with the Leadville Unit, Resurrection Mine, Irene Shaft, and Yak Tunnel. Later workings connected into the extensive older underground network of the Leadville district.
The modern tailings impoundment and related surface features are components of the larger mine-and-mill complex rather than the whole operation.

sites.name: Champion Mill
overview: Champion Mill was the processing end of the Mount Champion mining system west of Leadville. Ore moved from the high-elevation mine to the mill by a long aerial tramway, making the surviving mill, tram towers, and upper mine workings parts of one connected industrial landscape.

Period mining literature describes the mill at roughly 12,000 feet elevation and the mine above 13,000 feet. The operation treated gold-bearing sulphide ore that could also carry silver, copper, and lead values before concentrates or selected high-grade ore were sent toward Leadville smelters.

timeline.text: The Mount Champion property was discovered, although substantial development came later.
The Mount Champion Mining Company acquired the property and began major development of the mine, mill, and aerial-tram system.
The Mount Champion Mining Company was incorporated during the period when the operation was being developed into a substantial mine-and-mill complex.
The operation entered its principal production period. The aerial tram carried ore from the high mine workings to the mill in Halfmoon Valley.

Engineering and Mining Journal published a technical account of practice at the Mount Champion mill, documenting the unusually high-elevation operating conditions and the connected mine-to-mill tramway.
Regular production ended as transportation and operating economics made continued shipment and treatment unprofitable.
The property saw a brief later reopening before shutting down again.
The large mill structure and surviving pieces of the aerial-tram landscape remain strong visual evidence of how the remote mine and processing plant functioned together.

moreHistory: The Champion site is best understood as a system rather than as one building. The mine occupied the high slopes of Mount Champion, while the mill stood far below in Halfmoon Valley. An aerial tram roughly 6,100 feet long linked the two, allowing ore to move across terrain that would have made wagon haulage extremely difficult.

A Mining History Association account describes the underground mine as three drift tunnels totaling about 10,000 feet of workings, with roughly thirty men employed underground during the principal operating period. The same account describes sixteen men working at the mill.

The mill used a multi-stage crushing and concentration process. Documented equipment included jaw and disc crushers, screens, a ball mill and tube mill, classifiers, amalgamating copper plates, a thickener, concentrating tables, an elevator, and additional gravity-concentration equipment. This machinery explains why the surviving structure was so large: it housed a sequence of processing steps rather than a single crusher.

Ore from the Mount Champion workings contained values chiefly in sulphides. Gold was important, with smaller silver values and occasional copper and lead. Selected high-grade ore could bypass some milling and be shipped toward Leadville smelters, while lower-grade material was concentrated at the mill before shipment.

The tramway is one of the defining features of the Champion complex. Historical descriptions note that it crossed very high terrain and used numerous wooden towers to carry buckets between the mine and mill. The surviving towers and tram-related remains are therefore not separate curiosities; they are evidence of the transportation system that made the mill practical.

Champion also illustrates the economic limits of remote high-country mining. Even with mechanized milling and aerial transport, the operation depended on the cost of moving ore and concentrates onward to Leadville. When those costs outweighed the value recovered, the main production period ended.

For Remnant identification, the mill should remain distinct from the upper Champion Mine workings while still being linked to them as components of the same historic operation. The mill, tramway, and mine tell different parts of the same extraction-to-processing story.

sites.name: Chrysolite Mine
overview: Chrysolite was one of the famous Fryer Hill mines that helped define Leadville’s late-1870s silver boom. Government mining reports place it among the important carbonate-ore workings on Fryer Hill, where rich lead-silver deposits were developed beneath a complex sequence of porphyry, limestone, and quartzite.

The mine is historically tied to Horace Tabor’s rise during the Leadville boom, but Remnant treats Chrysolite as its own mine rather than as an extension of the nearby Matchless or Little Pittsburg properties.

timeline.text: Chrysolite emerged during the first rush of major carbonate discoveries on Fryer Hill as Leadville’s silver boom accelerated.
The mine became one of the significant Fryer Hill producers documented in federal mining reports and detailed geological mapping.
Leadville mining continued through changing metal markets; government accounts record work on Chrysolite dumps as operators sought value from previously mined material.
Federal geological work documented the Chrysolite workings in detail, including the Roberts and Clark shaft areas and the complicated Fryer Hill ore geology.
Chrysolite remains an important reference point for interpreting Fryer Hill and the dense cluster of historic Leadville mines.

moreHistory: Fryer Hill was one of the most intensely developed parts of the Leadville district. Chrysolite worked the same broad carbonate-ore environment that made neighboring mines famous, but each property followed its own shafts, stopes, faults, and ore bodies.

USGS and earlier federal mining reports describe Fryer Hill as geologically complicated. Sheets of white and gray porphyry cut and displaced the favorable limestone units, and miners had to follow irregular replacement bodies rather than a simple vein.

Historic federal mapping specifically documents Chrysolite mine workings and later shaft development. Those records make the mine useful for understanding how Leadville operators used shafts and underground levels to chase ore through a difficult three-dimensional geologic setting.

Chrysolite is also part of the Horace Tabor story. Period and later mining histories connect Tabor with the property during the same extraordinary boom that produced fortunes from Little Pittsburg and other Fryer Hill mines.

For Remnant, Chrysolite should remain a separate site from Matchless, Little Pittsburg, and the broader Leadville district. The close spacing of those properties is part of the story: a relatively small hill contained numerous independently operated mines competing for access to rich carbonate ore.

sites.name: Climax Molybdenum Mine / Climax Mine
sites.componentType: World-Class Molybdenum Mine / Underground & Open-Pit Complex
overview: Climax is one of the world’s best-known molybdenum deposits and one of Colorado’s most important twentieth-century mining operations. The high-elevation complex at Fremont Pass evolved from underground mining into a very large open-pit and milling operation.
The site is especially useful for showing how mining technology, scale, and surface appearance changed from early underground development to modern bulk mining and flotation processing.

timeline.text: Claims were staked on Bartlett Mountain for mineralization that was later recognized as molybdenum ore.
Large-scale development accelerated during World War I as demand for molybdenum increased.
Production was suspended after wartime demand collapsed.
Production resumed after metallurgical improvements and new markets were developed.
Climax was operating at roughly 1,000–1,200 tons of ore per day and had become one of Colorado’s largest mining operations.
The mine expanded through extensive underground workings and later transitioned to large-scale open-pit mining and modern milling.
The modern Climax operation reopened after a closure period.

moreHistory: Molybdenite is the principal ore mineral at Climax, and the deposit became the type example for the rare class of Climax-type porphyry molybdenum deposits.

Historic components include major underground levels and tunnels, hoisting and haulage facilities, crushing and flotation systems, and later open-pit, concentrator, and tailings landscapes. These should be kept as linked components rather than treated as one building or portal.
Historic production figures should remain tied to the specific years and sources that reported them rather than being extrapolated into an unsupported lifetime total.

features.name: Historic Underground Mine System
features.note: Climax developed a very large underground mine before the later open-pit phase.

features.name: Open-Pit Mine and Modern Mill
features.note: The modern operation includes the open pit, concentrator, tailings and related industrial infrastructure.

sites.name: Hagerman Trestle
overview: The Hagerman Trestle was part of the Colorado Midland railroad’s difficult high-elevation route across the mountains west of Leadville. The railroad landscape around Hagerman Pass required major engineering works to overcome steep grades, snow, and rugged terrain.
The trestle should be understood as one component of the broader Colorado Midland route rather than as an isolated structure.

timeline.text: The Colorado Midland developed its high-country route west of Leadville as part of the railroad’s push across the Continental Divide.
Large timber trestles, cuts, grades, snow-control work, and tunnel infrastructure were used to carry trains through the Hagerman Pass landscape.
Period imagery documented the dramatic railroad engineering around Hagerman Pass, including trestle and snow-operation scenes.
The original railroad infrastructure fell out of use, but portions of the grade and structural remains continued to mark the former route.
The surviving railroad landscape helps interpret the engineering challenge of operating a mountain railroad at very high elevation.

moreHistory: Hagerman Pass presented severe operating problems: heavy winter snow, steep mountain terrain, high elevation, and the need to maintain a workable railroad grade.
The trestle was one of several engineering elements in the route. Tunnel approaches, grade, cuts, fills, snow-control operations, and other structures should be interpreted as related components.

The Library of Congress preserves a rights-cleared historical image of Colorado Midland snow-plow operations at Hagerman Pass. That image provides operating-era railroad context, but it should not be captioned as a direct photograph of the trestle unless the structure is actually shown.
A separate W.H. Jackson catalog reference documents that a trestle-specific historical view existed, further supporting the importance of the structure within the Hagerman route.

features.name: Hagerman Trestle
features.note: A major timber railroad structure associated with the Colorado Midland mountain route.

features.name: Colorado Midland Grade
features.note: The trestle is part of the broader high-elevation railroad grade.

features.name: Snow-Operation Landscape
features.note: Historic imagery documents the extreme snow conditions faced by railroad crews at Hagerman Pass.

sites.name: Ibex / Little Jonny Mine
overview: The Little Jonny was a major gold-producing working within the broader Ibex property on Breece Hill in the Leadville district.
Remnant preserves the relationship between the Little Jonny working and the Ibex property while keeping the individual mine component identifiable.

timeline.text: Major development expanded the Ibex / Little Jonny workings during Leadville’s later gold-producing period.
USGS historical mapping records substantial gold production from the Ibex / Little Jonny operation during this period.
Historical records document a Denver & Rio Grande railroad connection serving the Ibex operation.
The property remained part of the heavily developed Breece Hill mining landscape.

moreHistory: USGS and Colorado mining-history sources identify the Little Jonny as a significant gold-development component of the Ibex property.
The property is also associated with J.J. Brown management in the broader historical record, linking the industrial history of Breece Hill with well-known Leadville personalities.
The 1898 railroad connection illustrates how large mine properties depended on transportation infrastructure for ore, supplies, and equipment.

production.summary: Historical federal sources describe substantial gold production from the Ibex / Little Jonny operation between 1893 and 1923. Exact totals should be shown only when a source-specific figure is entered into the registry.
production.note: The current app text intentionally avoids inventing an exact production total where the registry summary does not provide one.

sites.name: Leadville Mine Drainage Tunnel / LMDT
sites.category: Mining Infrastructure / Federal Engineering / Environmental History
overview: The Leadville Mine Drainage Tunnel is a major federal engineering feature built beneath the Leadville mining district to lower groundwater in underground workings and improve access to mineral reserves. It later became a central part of the district’s water-treatment and environmental history.
The tunnel, outlet, treatment plant, connected mine workings, and monitoring locations are related components and should not be treated as a single visible structure.

timeline.text: The U.S. Bureau of Mines constructed the first section of the tunnel during World War II to drain mine workings and improve mineral access.
The tunnel was extended during renewed Korean War demand for metals.
The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation acquired the tunnel.
A modern treatment plant was commissioned to treat metal-bearing tunnel discharge before it entered the Arkansas River headwaters.
The tunnel and treatment system remain important parts of the environmental and engineering history of the Leadville district.

moreHistory: Federal sources describe the LMDT as approximately two miles long. USGS studies documented substantial lowering of mine-water levels after tunnel drainage began.
The tunnel was later considered as a possible water source for the Fryingpan-Arkansas Project, but existing water-rights claims prevented that use.
Because mine drainage contains dissolved metals, treatment of the discharge became a long-term federal responsibility and an important chapter in the post-mining history of the district.

features.name: Leadville Mine Drainage Tunnel
features.note: The underground tunnel is the principal drainage feature beneath the historic mining district.

features.name: Water Treatment System
features.note: The modern treatment system addresses metal-bearing drainage from the historic mine network.

sites.name: Maid of Erin Mine
overview: The Maid of Erin was one of the named mines in Leadville’s dense Carbonate Hill mining landscape. Its history overlaps with neighboring properties but the mine remains a distinct Remnant site.
The property is useful for understanding how Leadville’s mines changed through operating, leasing, dump-processing, and later environmental-remediation periods.

timeline.text: The Maid of Erin operated as part of the heavily developed Carbonate Hill district.
Historical property records document leasing and later processing of mine-dump material.
EPA historic-property documentation records consolidation and remediation of waste associated with Maid of Erin, Wolftone, and Mahala areas.
The site is interpreted as a distinct mine component within a tightly packed historic and remediated mining landscape.

moreHistory: EPA California Gulch documentation provides unusually useful information because it preserves both operating history and later changes to the physical mining landscape.
Maid of Erin should not be merged with Wolftone or other nearby Carbonate Hill properties simply because their histories and remediation areas overlap.
USGS Leadville district studies provide the larger geologic and ore-deposit framework needed to understand why so many mines were concentrated in this area.

sites.name: Matchless Mine
overview: The Matchless Mine is one of Leadville’s best-known historic silver properties, important both for its role in the mining industry and for its association with Horace Tabor and Elizabeth “Baby Doe” Tabor.
The surviving complex preserves recognizable mine infrastructure that helps explain underground extraction, surface hoisting, ore handling, and support functions.

timeline.text: The Matchless property became associated with Horace Tabor during Leadville’s rapid silver boom.
The mine operated during Leadville’s major silver-production era and became part of Tabor’s mining fortune.
The national silver crisis badly damaged Leadville’s silver economy and Tabor’s finances.
Horace Tabor died after the collapse of much of his former fortune.
Baby Doe Tabor remained closely associated with the property.
Surviving mine buildings and equipment make the Matchless one of the most recognizable historic mining complexes in Leadville.

moreHistory: History Colorado recognizes the Matchless for both industrial and social significance.
The complex includes the No. 6 shaft area, headframe and hoisting infrastructure, a powder magazine, cabin, and other surface features.
The Tabor story turned the mine into a symbol of both the extraordinary wealth and the volatility of Colorado’s silver era.
Baby Doe’s long association with the property helped preserve the Matchless in public memory well after the mine’s peak industrial period.

features.name: No. 6 Shaft and Headframe Area
features.note: A central surviving component of the surface complex.

features.name: Hoisting Infrastructure
features.note: The hoisting system illustrates movement between surface and underground workings.

features.name: Powder Magazine
features.note: A distinct support component of mine operations.

features.name: Historic Cabin
features.note: The cabin contributes to the social history of the property and its Tabor association.

sites.name: Oro City & California Gulch Placer Diggings
overview: Oro City and the California Gulch placer diggings represent the early gold-rush phase of the Leadville story, before the district became famous for later hard-rock silver, lead, zinc, and gold mining.
Remnant distinguishes old Oro City, later Oro City components, and the placer-mining landscape instead of treating the entire gulch as one undifferentiated site.

timeline.text: Gold discoveries in California Gulch triggered rapid placer mining and settlement in the Leadville area.
Oro City developed around the booming gulch while miners worked stream gravels and other placer deposits.
As easy placer deposits declined, the district’s economic focus shifted toward hard-rock mining and new communities.
W.G. Chamberlain photographed hydraulic mining in California Gulch, preserving a rights-cleared image of the placer landscape.

moreHistory: USGS historic mapping distinguishes multiple Oro City place references and the broader placer landscape, which is why Remnant keeps these components separate.
The California Gulch placer story is important because it explains the first major mining rush that preceded Leadville’s better-known carbonate-ore boom.
The cleared 1878 Library of Congress stereograph provides direct historical evidence of hydraulic placer mining in California Gulch.

sites.name: Stumptown Mining Camp
overview: Stumptown was a mining camp in South Evans Gulch that grew around the mines east of Leadville. Mining History Association material traces its beginning to the 1879 discovery of the Little Ellen Mine and identifies the settlement as an active mining community into the twentieth century.
The camp is best understood as a cluster: homes and camp structures were surrounded by individual mines including the Little Ellen, Ollie Reed, Favorite, Silent Friend, and nearby tunnel workings.

timeline.text: Discovery of the Little Ellen Mine helped start the settlement first known as South Evans and later as Stumptown.
The camp developed alongside a dense group of mines in South Evans Gulch during Leadville’s major mining era.
Mining continued around the camp, with several neighboring properties remaining active as ore types and markets changed.
The nearby Silent Friend Mine was an important producer of oxidized zinc ores during this period.
Long-term mining activity declined and the settlement was largely abandoned, while mine ruins and landscape traces remained.
Stumptown survives primarily as a historic mining landscape where camp history and multiple mine sites overlap.

moreHistory: Stumptown illustrates how Leadville’s mining camps often formed directly beside groups of producing properties rather than as isolated towns. Workers could live near the mines that employed them, and the camp’s identity was tied closely to activity in South Evans Gulch.

The Little Ellen discovery is central to the camp’s origin. Later historical interpretation links Stumptown with the Ollie Reed, Favorite, Silent Friend, Little Ellen, Little Bob, and St. Louis Tunnel areas, showing how many separate workings contributed to one community landscape.

The camp also has a well-known social-history connection: Margaret “Molly” Brown and her husband J. J. Brown lived in the Stumptown area early in their marriage before the family became nationally prominent.

Remnant treats Stumptown as the parent camp record. Individual mines remain separate components when they have enough evidence to support their own identification record, preventing the camp entry from becoming a catch-all for every ruin in South Evans Gulch.

sites.name: Tucson Mine Ruins
overview: The Tucson Mine was a substantial Iron Hill operation in the Leadville district. Historic accounts describe deep shaft development and later mining of silver, lead, zinc, and zinc-carbonate ores, while surviving heavy foundations and ore-handling remains indicate the scale of the surface plant.
The Tucson should be interpreted as one mine within the broader Iron Silver Mining Company landscape, not as a label for every nearby Iron Hill working.

timeline.text: The Tucson became one of the developed Iron Hill workings as Leadville operators expanded underground through shafts and inclines.
The Tucson shaft reached roughly 1,100 feet, reflecting substantial underground development.
Historic mining literature reported very high-grade silver assays from lower levels of the mine.
Considerable mining continued, with lead- and zinc-sulfide ores forming an important part of production.
Several attempts were made to reopen or sustain the property, but none produced a lasting revival.
The upper part of the shaft was reopened to reach a remaining zinc-carbonate, or smithsonite, ore body.
Large ore-bin remnants, dumps, and heavy hoist foundations remain useful identification clues for the former mine complex.

moreHistory: Iron Hill was one of Leadville’s major mining zones. The Tucson developed within a dense group of Iron Silver Mining Company properties where separate shafts and claims tapped related but locally complex ore bodies.

Historical descriptions of the Tucson emphasize the depth of the shaft and the changing character of the ore. Silver-rich material was reported from deeper levels, while lead and zinc sulfides became important during the 1910s.

The 1940 reopening targeted smithsonite, a zinc carbonate left from earlier mining. That episode shows how operators repeatedly reconsidered old workings when metal prices, processing methods, or knowledge of remaining ore changed.

Surviving surface features are especially useful for identification. Large ore-storage remnants and substantial concrete hoist foundations indicate that Tucson was not a minor prospect; it required heavy equipment to move ore and workers through a deep shaft system.
For Remnant, nearby Iron Hill mines should remain separate records. Shared ownership or underground relationships do not mean every surviving ruin belongs to the Tucson Mine.

sites.name: Twin Lakes Historic District / Historic Twin Lakes Village
overview: Twin Lakes Historic District preserves one of Lake County’s best surviving late-nineteenth-century mountain villages. Its compact collection of historic buildings reflects the community that served travelers, residents, miners, and visitors moving through the Upper Arkansas and Independence Pass region.

The district is separate from the Interlaken Resort complex across the lake. Remnant treats Twin Lakes as the historic village parent record while preserving individual buildings for possible future sub-site expansion.

timeline.text: Twin Lakes was already recognized as a mountain destination and transportation setting during the early mining era; surviving historic photography documents the landscape by the 1870s.
Most principal contributing buildings associated with the historic district date from the final two decades of the nineteenth century.
The village served a regional network of mining, transportation, lodging, commerce, fishing, and mountain travel rather than functioning as a single mine camp.
The village retained enough historic fabric to preserve a recognizable nineteenth-century mountain-community character.
The historic district remains identifiable through its concentration of log buildings, gabled roofs, village-scale setting, and relationship to Twin Lakes and the surrounding mountains.

moreHistory: History Colorado describes Twin Lakes as one of the best remaining examples of a late-1800s Colorado mountain village. Many of the principal contributing buildings are log construction with gabled roofs, giving the district a coherent visual character.

Twin Lakes occupied an important position between the Upper Arkansas Valley and routes crossing the high country. Its history therefore mixes mining-era transportation and commerce with lodging, tourism, fishing, and community life.

Early landscape photographs are valuable evidence because they show that Twin Lakes had already become a recognized destination during the nineteenth century. They provide context for the village even when a photograph does not identify one specific surviving building.

Interlaken Resort is historically related but physically and functionally separate. Keeping the two records distinct prevents the resort’s development history from being incorrectly assigned to the Twin Lakes village.

For Remnant, the district works best as a parent community record. Individual houses or commercial buildings are not part of the current app scope, but their research can remain available for possible future sub-sites.

sites.name: Wolftone Mine
overview: The Wolftone was an important Carbonate Hill mine whose history extended beyond Leadville’s classic silver era into the later zinc economy.
It was connected historically with the broader A.M.W. operating context but remains a distinct mine from Maid of Erin, Adams, and neighboring properties.

timeline.text: The Wolftone developed as part of Leadville’s densely mined Carbonate Hill area.
EPA historical documentation records renewed operation after the mine was unwatered.
The property became important in Leadville’s shift toward zinc production.
Historical records document reprocessing of mine-dump material.
Waste from Wolftone and nearby mine areas was consolidated as part of California Gulch remediation work.

moreHistory: The Wolftone illustrates how one mine can pass through several industrial phases: underground production, changes in target commodities, dump reprocessing, and environmental remediation.
EPA records are especially useful for reconstructing both the operational history and later physical changes to the property.
USGS district studies provide the broader geological framework for the lead, silver, and zinc ores that shaped Carbonate Hill mining.

sites.name: Agwalt Tunnel
overview: Agwalt Tunnel is a documented historic mine tunnel in the Leadville Mining District. Federal mineral records identify it as a gold property with lead and zinc also reported, while USGS-derived topographic records preserve the named tunnel on the Mount Sherman quadrangle.
Period mining reporting shows that the Agwalt Mining Company was actively driving the tunnel in 1895 as a major underground development intended to intersect the Little Johnny ore chute.

timeline.text: The Engineering and Mining Journal reported that the Agwalt Mining Company, headed by mining man Tingley S. Wood, had driven the Agwalt tunnel about 3,300 feet and was advancing it to cut the Little Johnny ore chute; the company planned to use a diamond drill to locate the ore body after completion.

moreHistory: USGS Mineral Resources Data System information reproduced by Western Mining History identifies Agwalt Tunnel in Lake County's Leadville district, lists gold as the primary commodity with lead and zinc also present, and gives an approximate mapped position near 39.2375, -106.24333.

USGS-derived topographic place data independently identifies Agwalt Tunnel Mine on the Mount Sherman quadrangle near 39.23721, -106.24363. The close agreement between the mineral record and topographic mapping provides a defensible site-level identification point without implying that a surviving portal has been field-surveyed, is open, or is accessible today.

sites.name: Agassiz Mine
sites.location: Fryer Hill, Leadville Mining District, Lake County
overview: Agassiz Mine is a documented historic underground mine on Fryer Hill in the Leadville mining district. A USGS Mineral Resources Data System record places the site near 39.24833, -106.27111 and classifies the patented property as a past producer with zinc recorded as a commodity.

timeline.event: A Leadville newspaper's weekly ore-output report listed the Agassiz among producing mines.
The U.S. Geological Survey's Geology and Mining Industry of Leadville documented the district and mapped mining on Fryer Hill.
USGS Professional Paper 148 provided a later comprehensive account of Leadville geology and ore deposits and is retained in the federal Agassiz mine record's bibliography.

moreHistory: The reviewed evidence consistently places the Agassiz on Fryer Hill in the Leadville district. The federal mine record identifies a patented, underground, past-producing property and supplies a specific mapped site point.

Available sources do not establish a dependable operator chronology, production total, detailed workings description, or present condition. The mapped point is a historic site-level reference and should not be treated as a surveyed safe or accessible opening.

sites.name: Adams Shaft
sites.location: Leadville mining district, north of Leadville
sites.componentDetail: Deep Mine Shaft / Wolftone-Area Underground Workings
overview: Adams Shaft is a documented historic mine shaft in the Leadville mining district, mapped north of Leadville near the Matchless and Wolftone-area workings.

Period reporting described the shaft at about 460 feet deep in 1886. Later district reporting shows it remained part of the underground mining network, and a 1949 U.S. Bureau of Mines investigation specifically included Adams among the Leadville shafts examined, mapped, and sampled.

timeline.text: The Carbonate Chronicle reported the Adams shaft at about 460 feet deep, alongside the neighboring Result shaft.
Leadville district reporting said the Adams shaft would be used to carry on mining work as zinc deposits developed through the Wolftone shaft extended into adjoining workings.
U.S. Bureau of Mines Report of Investigations 4518 included Adams Shaft in its examination, mapping, and sampling of Leadville mine shafts and underground workings.

moreHistory: Adams Shaft belonged to Leadville's dense network of underground workings rather than to the unrelated Hub Gulch adit previously described in the registry.

The mapped identification point at approximately 39.250545, -106.273635 corresponds to the named Adams Shaft shown in USGS-derived topographic data. It is a site-level historic identification point, not a field survey of present shaft conditions.
Historic mine workings can be unstable and dangerous. Visitors should remain on lawful public routes, respect closures and private property, and never enter or approach an open shaft.

timeline.event: A Leadville newspaper retrospective identified the Aetna among lodes on the southwestern part of Carbonate Hill.
The U.S. Geological Survey's Professional Paper 148 documented the geology and ore deposits of the Leadville district; that report is retained in the later federal mine record's bibliography.
The U.S. Bureau of Mines reported the Aetna record that was later updated within the USGS Mineral Resources Data System.

moreHistory: The reviewed evidence consistently places the Aetna in the Leadville district on Carbonate Hill, not at Longfellow Gulch. The federal mine record identifies an underground, patented, past-producing property and supplies a specific ore-body coordinate.

Available desk sources do not establish a dependable production total, operator chronology, detailed workings description, or present condition. The mapped point is a historic site-level reference and should not be treated as a surveyed safe or accessible opening.

sites.name: Chrysolite Mine
sites.componentDetail: Historic Fryer Hill silver-lead carbonate mine
overview: Chrysolite was one of the famous Fryer Hill mines that helped define Leadville’s late-1870s silver boom. Government mining reports place it among the important carbonate-ore workings on Fryer Hill, where rich lead-silver deposits were developed beneath a complex sequence of porphyry, limestone, and quartzite.
The mine is historically tied to Horace Tabor’s rise during the Leadville boom, but Remnant treats Chrysolite as its own mine rather than as an extension of nearby properties.

timeline.text: Chrysolite emerged during the first rush of major carbonate discoveries on Fryer Hill as Leadville’s silver boom accelerated.
The mine became one of the significant Fryer Hill producers documented in federal mining reports and detailed geological mapping.
Leadville mining continued through changing metal markets; government accounts record work on Chrysolite dumps as operators sought value from previously mined material.
Federal geological work documented the Chrysolite workings in detail, including shaft areas and the complicated Fryer Hill ore geology.

moreHistory: Fryer Hill was one of the most intensely developed parts of the Leadville district. Chrysolite worked the same broad carbonate-ore environment that made neighboring mines famous, but each property followed its own shafts, stopes, faults, and ore bodies.

Historic federal mapping documents Chrysolite mine workings and later shaft development, making the mine useful for understanding how Leadville operators chased ore through a difficult three-dimensional geologic setting.
